lesson.title: Smooth Enough to Have a Slope
lesson.summary: Explains why differentiability implies continuity but not the reverse, contrasting a sharp corner with a vertical tangent using a rigorous limit check on x to the two thirds power.
lesson.body:
Differentiability is the property of having a well defined derivative, and understanding it fully means understanding its relationship to continuity, a concept it depends on but does not simply repeat. Every differentiable function is continuous: if f prime of a exists, the graph of f cannot have a jump or a hole at x = a, because the existence of a finite limiting slope forces the function values on either side of a to converge to f(a) as well. This fact, differentiability implies continuity, is a genuine theorem, not just a coincidence seen in examples. This directional link, from differentiability to continuity, only runs one way, which is the entire subject of the paragraphs that follow.

The converse, however, is false, and that gap is important. A function can be continuous everywhere and still fail to be differentiable at particular points, which the absolute value function already demonstrated with its sharp corner at 0. Corners are one way differentiability can fail while continuity survives, but they are not the only way. A vertical tangent line is another: the curve is unbroken and continuous, yet its slope becomes infinite at one point, so no finite derivative exists there.

Consider f(x) = x raised to the two thirds power, meaning the cube root of x, then squared, evaluated at x = 0. This function is continuous everywhere, including at 0, where it takes the value 0. Applying the limit definition at that point: f prime of 0 equals the limit as h approaches 0 of [h to the two thirds power minus 0] divided by h, which simplifies to h to the two thirds power divided by h, or equivalently h to the negative one third power, which is the same as 1 divided by the cube root of h. As h approaches 0 from the positive side, the cube root of h is a small positive number, so 1 divided by it grows without bound toward positive infinity. As h approaches 0 from the negative side, the cube root of h is a small negative number, so 1 divided by it plunges without bound toward negative infinity. Neither one sided limit settles on a finite number, so f prime of 0 does not exist, even though the graph never breaks or jumps: it simply becomes vertical at that single point.

This distinction, corners versus vertical tangents, both defeat differentiability but in different geometric ways: a corner has two different finite one sided slopes that disagree, while a vertical tangent has one sided slopes that both run off to infinity in the same or opposite directions. Either way, the underlying test is identical: differentiability requires the difference quotient limit to exist and be a finite number, from both sides at once, agreeing exactly.

Keeping continuity and differentiability distinct matters because many later results, including ones about maximum and minimum values and about approximating curves with straight lines, require differentiability specifically, and simply confirming a function is continuous is not sufficient grounds to apply them.
